prompt_text: How to run a peer-to-peer fundraising campaign
response_text:
A peer-to-peer (P2P) fundraising campaign works best when you move in clear stages: define a specific goal, choose the right platform, recruit and equip a core group of ambassadors, launch with strong branding and a promotion plan, actively coach fundraisers during the campaign, and close with a strong finish and thorough stewardship of new donors.[1][2][7]

Below is a practical, step‑by‑step playbook you can adapt for almost any nonprofit or cause.

---

## 1. Clarify your campaign strategy

Before you invite anyone to fundraise, get crystal clear on what you’re doing and why.

- **Define the purpose and use of funds.** Decide exactly what you are funding (e.g., “scholarships for 50 students” vs. “general operations for 6 months”).[1][2]  
- **Set a realistic, specific goal.** Estimate costs, then match them against your audience size and typical gift sizes to set a campaign total and optional sub‑goals (e.g., “50 fundraisers, each raising $500”).[2]  
- **Decide the structure.** Examples:  
  - Time‑bound campaign (30‑day push, Giving Day, birthday month)[2][4]  
  - Event‑based (walk/run, bike challenge, gaming marathon)[1][7]  
  - Always‑on/rolling P2P (ongoing DIY campaigns hosted on your site)[2][6]  
- **Define success metrics.** Beyond dollars: number of new donors, average raised per fundraiser, % of fundraisers who get at least one gift, email signups, etc.[6][7]

Having this upfront avoids confusion later and makes your pitch to fundraisers much stronger.[1]

---

## 2. Plan logistics and internal roles

Treat P2P like a mini‑product launch.

- **Clarify internal ownership.** Decide who leads: one staff owner for the whole campaign, plus point people for tech, communications, and stewardship.[1]  
- **Map the timeline.** Include:  
  - Prep (2–6 weeks): platform setup, branding, recruiting core fundraisers  
  - Soft launch: core supporters start fundraising  
  - Public launch: broader promotion to your full audience  
  - Engagement phase: regular updates and coaching  
  - Final push: last 3–7 days  
  - Stewardship: 2–4 weeks after campaign  
- **If there’s an event, plan it fully.** Venue or virtual setup, permits, schedule, speakers, and contingency plans.[1][2]  
- **Decide tracking and reporting.** How often you’ll review performance and what reports you’ll pull (leaderboards, inactive fundraisers, top donors).[1][2]

---

## 3. Choose and set up your P2P tech

You need software that makes it easy for supporters to set up personal pages and for you to track results.

- **Select a platform** that supports:  
  - Individual and team pages  
  - Easy page setup for supporters (ideally in minutes)  
  - Mobile‑friendly donation forms  
  - Integrated email/social sharing tools  
  - Real‑time totals and leaderboards  
  - Data export into your CRM or database[1][3][6][7]  
- **Configure core pages.**  
  - Main campaign page with goal, impact explanation, compelling imagery, and video if possible.[2][4]  
  - Branded checkout/donation page with simple, secure payment and suggested gift amounts tied to impact.[2][7]  
- **Test everything before launch.** Run test donations, create a sample fundraiser page, test emails and texts, and confirm notifications work.[1][2]

---

## 4. Recruit the right fundraisers first

P2P rises and falls on the quality and enthusiasm of your fundraisers.

- **Identify “core supporters.”** Start with people who already love you: board members, long‑time donors, volunteers, program alumni, active social followers, staff, and partners.[1][2][3]  
- **Invite them personally.** Call or send individualized emails inviting them into an “inner circle” to help launch the campaign.[2] Personal outreach converts far better than mass email.  
- **Clarify the ask.** Be specific: “Will you create a fundraising page, share it 3–5 times, and aim to raise $500?”[1][7]  
- **Recruit broadly after your core.** Once your initial group is set up and raising, invite your wider audience by email, social media, and at events.[2][4]

Aim to spend at least a week seeding the campaign with your core fundraisers before full public launch to build early momentum.[2]

---

## 5. Build a strong campaign brand and story

People give to people, but a cohesive campaign brand makes everything feel credible and exciting.

- **Create a simple, memorable theme.** Title + short pitch that explains the campaign and why it matters now (your “30‑second elevator pitch”).[2]  
- **Define core messaging.**  
  - What problem are you solving?  
  - What specific impact a donation creates?  
  - Why urgency (time limit, match, milestone)?[1][2][7]  
- **Develop consistent visuals.**  
  - Campaign logo or mark  
  - Color palette and fonts aligned with your org brand  
  - Templates for social graphics, email headers, and personal fundraiser pages[1][2][4]  

Use this brand and message everywhere: website, emails, social, and supporter toolkits.[1][4]

---

## 6. Plan your marketing and communications

You need a central communications plan; fundraisers amplify it.

- **Create a channel plan.** Decide how you will use:  
  - Email (campaign announcements, updates, coaching)[1][2]  
  - Social media (daily or near‑daily posts with stories and milestones)[1][2][9]  
  - Website and blog (stories, impact updates)[2]  
  - SMS/text (short reminders for key moments, if appropriate)  
- **Build a content calendar.** Include:  
  - Teaser posts before launch  
  - Launch announcement  
  - Mid‑campaign impact stories and progress updates  
  - Final‑week and final‑day urgency pushes  
  - Post‑campaign thanks and results[1][2][7][9]  
- **Prepare content in advance.** Draft as many posts, emails, and graphics as possible ahead of time so you can focus on live engagement during the campaign.[2]

---

## 7. Equip fundraisers with a toolkit

The more you make it “turn‑key,” the more they will do.

Provide a **peer‑to‑peer toolkit** that includes:[1][7][8]

- **Step‑by‑step setup instructions** for their fundraising page with screenshots.  
- **Sample copy** they can customize:  
  - Page headline and story text  
  - Email and DM templates asking for support  
  - Short social media captions and texts  
- **Branded visuals** sized for major platforms.  
- **Talking points and FAQs** about your organization and the campaign.  
- **Best practices** on:  
  - Making the first gift to their own page to “seed” it  
  - Sharing personal stories tied to the cause  
  - When and how often to ask (e.g., launch, mid‑campaign, final push)[1][7][9]  

Consider hosting a **kickoff session** (live or virtual) to walk fundraisers through goals, platform features, and outreach tips, and to answer questions.[9]

---

## 8. Launch and build momentum

Don’t just “turn it on” – orchestrate a launch.

- **Soft launch with core fundraisers.** Get their pages live and have them secure a few early gifts before public promotion.[2]  
- **Public launch day.**  
  - Send a launch email to your full list.  
  - Announce on all social channels and pin posts.  
  - Ask partners and sponsors to share.  
- **Show visible progress quickly.** Promote leaderboards, early totals, and any matching‑gift periods to excite supporters.[2][7]  

If you have a match (e.g., a $10,000 corporate gift), use it strategically as a time‑limited challenge period to energize outreach.[2]

---

## 9. Actively manage and support during the campaign

P2P campaigns require hands‑on management, especially in the middle weeks when momentum can dip.

- **Monitor performance regularly.** Track:  
  - Who has created pages but has no gifts  
  - Top fundraisers and teams  
  - Overall progress vs. goal  
- **Segment your communications.**  
  - To **inactive fundraisers**: send practical tips and encouragement to help them get started.[2]  
  - To **active/top fundraisers**: send personal thanks, recognize them publicly, and give advanced tips.[2][9]  
- **Provide ongoing content.** Share stories, photos, short videos from the field, stats, and progress graphics that fundraisers can repost.[2][7]  
- **Celebrate milestones.** Recognize when you hit 25%, 50%, 75% of your goal, and individual milestones for fundraisers (e.g., first donation, goal hit).[1][2][9]

Aim for 1–2 campaign emails per week and multiple social updates per day during the heart of the campaign, calibrated to your audience so it doesn’t feel like spam.[2]

---

## 10. Drive a strong final push

Many campaigns raise a large percentage of funds in the last few days.
